## Setup

```{python}
import pandas as pd

url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/eurovision_contestants.csv'
eurovision = pd.read_csv(url)
```

## Part 1: What is in this file, and what is missing from it

**1. How many rows and columns? What are the column names, and what is the range of `year`?**

```{python}
print(eurovision.shape)
print(list(eurovision.columns))
print(eurovision['year'].min(), eurovision['year'].max())
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**1,603 rows and 21 columns, covering 1956 to 2020.** The unit of a row is one country's entry in
one contest, not one contest, which is why there are 1,603 rows for 65 years.

The span of 65 years contains 65 distinct values of `year`, so every year in the range is
represented in the file, including the one that did not happen. Of the 21 columns, most describe
a result rather than a song: place and points in the final, place and points in the semi-final,
and since 2016 the jury and televote components of each.
:::

**2. Run `.isnull().sum()`. Several columns are null on well over a thousand of the 1,603 rows.
Pick two of them and, in a markdown cell, propose an explanation for each that has nothing to do
with anybody making a mistake.**

```{python}
eurovision.isnull().sum()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Both of the worst columns are null because the thing they measure did not exist yet.**

`sf_num` is null on 1,046 rows. The 557 rows where it is present all fall in 2004 or later, which
is when the contest introduced a semi-final. Before 2004 there was no semi-final to number, so
`place_sf`, `points_sf` and `running_sf` are null on 1,081 rows for the same reason.

`points_tele_final` and `points_jury_final` are null on 1,499 rows. The 104 rows where they are
present are all from 2016 to 2019, which is when the contest began publishing the televote and
the jury vote as two separate scores. Every earlier contest recorded a single combined score, and
nobody went back afterwards to split the old results in two.

A null can mean "not recorded", but in this file it usually means "not applicable", and neither
one is anybody's mistake. Dropping every row with a null here would leave you with almost nothing.
:::

**3. `points_final` is the column the rest of this exercise depends on, and it is null on 295
rows. Group by `year` and count the non-null `points_final` values in each. Look at the last few
years.**

```{python}
eurovision.groupby('year')['points_final'].count().tail(6)
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**The recent years sit at 26 or 27 finalists each, and then 2020 reports 0.** Note that `.count()`
counts non-null values, which is why it is the right method here: 26 is the number of countries
that reached the final and were scored, not the number that entered.
:::

**4. One of the years you just printed has a count of zero. Which one, and what happened? (You
may look this up. It is the only thing you are asked to look up in this exercise.)**

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**2020.** The contest was cancelled in March 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic, the first
cancellation in its history. The 41 entries are in the file with their performers and songs
because they had been selected before the cancellation, but no country ever performed and no
points were ever awarded, so `points_final` and `place_contest` are null on all 41 rows.

A second year also has a count of zero, and `.tail(6)` hides it. Print the head of the same series:

```{python}
eurovision.groupby('year')['points_final'].count().head(6)
```

**1956 also has a count of zero**, on 12 entries, and for a completely different reason: the
scores of the first contest were never published. Only the winner was announced. The two zeros
look identical in the output and have completely different causes: in 2020 no contest took place,
and in 1956 the contest took place and the numbers were never released.
:::

**5. Build a table called `contests` that excludes that year, using the filter pattern and
ending the line with `.copy()`. How many rows does it have?**

```{python}
contests = eurovision[eurovision['year'] != 2020].copy()
contests.shape
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**1,562 rows**, exactly 41 fewer than the 1,603 you started with, which confirms you removed the
2020 entries and nothing else. Whenever you filter, work out the row count you expect before you
run the line and then check it, because a filter that quietly matched more or less than you meant
usually shows up first as a number you did not predict.

Note that 1956 is still in `contests`. Its 12 rows have null `points_final`, so every mean and
count in the rest of the practice ignores them without saying so, which is the behaviour you want
here: pandas skips nulls in `.mean()` and `.count()` rather than treating them as zero.
:::

## Part 2: Decades

**6. Add a `decade` column. Divide `year` by ten, convert the result to an integer, and multiply
by ten. `.astype(int)` truncates toward zero, which is exactly what you want here. Then count the
entries in each decade.**

```{python}
contests['decade'] = (contests['year'] / 10).astype(int) * 10

contests['decade'].value_counts().sort_index()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**The count rises from 43 entries in the 1950s to 408 in the 2010s, roughly a tenfold increase.**
Some of the rise is real growth in the number of competing countries, but part of it is an artifact
of the bin: the 1950s decade holds only four contests, 1956 to 1959, while every later decade holds
ten. A per-decade total is not comparable across decades unless you also know how many contests
each decade contains.
:::

**7. Count the entries in each year from 2000 to 2007. What changes abruptly? In which year? In a
markdown cell, say what a sudden jump in entries per contest would do to a comparison of
average scores between the 1990s and the 2010s.**

```{python}
contests.groupby('year')['to_country'].count().loc[2000:2007]
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**The field jumps from 26 entries in 2003 to 36 in 2004, and keeps growing to 42 by 2007.**
2004 is the year the semi-final was introduced, the same 2004 that first fills in `sf_num`.
Once countries no longer all had to fit into one evening, many more of them could enter.

The jump is a serious problem for any comparison of average scores. Points are awarded by the
competing countries, so a larger field means more voters, which means more points in circulation,
which raises every score whether or not any song improved. A 2010s average and a 1990s average are
measured on scales that differ by roughly a factor of two in the number of voters, so comparing
them directly measures the size of the contest rather than the quality of the entries.
:::

## Part 3: The best country of each decade

**8. Build a table with one row per decade, holding the country with the highest average
`points_final` in that decade, how many scored finals that average came from, and the average
itself.**

```{python}
decade_winners_list = []

for decade, decade_data in contests.groupby('decade'):
    country_avg = decade_data.groupby('to_country')['points_final'].agg(['count', 'mean'])
    country_avg = country_avg.reset_index()
    top_country = country_avg.sort_values('mean', ascending=False).head(1).copy()
    top_country['decade'] = decade
    decade_winners_list.append(top_country)

decade_winners = pd.concat(decade_winners_list, ignore_index=True)

decade_winners[['decade', 'to_country', 'count', 'mean']]
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Seven rows and four columns: France takes the 1950s, the United Kingdom the 1960s and 1970s,
Ireland the 1980s and 1990s, Serbia the 2000s and Bulgaria the 2010s.** The `count` column should
read 3, 10, 10, 9, 10, 2 and 3 down the page, and the `mean` column 19.7, 23.1, 93.2, 99.2,
119.2, 214.0 and 362.7. If your table names the same seven countries against the same seven
decades, you built it correctly, even if your columns arrived in a different order or under
different names.

The pattern is the one we used this morning: build the pieces, collect them in a list, and stack
the list once at the end. Each pass through the loop builds a one-row DataFrame, the list collects
them, and the single `pd.concat()` after the loop stacks all seven rows into one table.
`ignore_index=True` matters more here than it did this morning, because each of those rows kept
whatever row label it happened to have inside its own decade's sorted table, so without it the
finished table is numbered 3, 16, 20, 9, 13, 37, 8 rather than 0 through 6, and nothing stops two
decades landing on the same label.

Two things can go wrong here and still leave you with a table that looks perfectly reasonable.
Leaving `ascending=False` out of `.sort_values()` sorts the other way, because ascending is the
default, and `.head(1)` then hands you the worst country of each decade in a table that is
otherwise the right size. Reaching for `.max()` on the `mean` column instead of `.head(1)` on the
sorted table gives you the number without the name, 362.7 for the 2010s with no Bulgaria attached
to it, and the name is half of what the question asked for.

`.reset_index()` is the line that turns `to_country` from the index into a column, which is what
lets the last line select it by name. A version of the loop that leaves the reset out stops with a
`KeyError` on `to_country` rather than returning a wrong table, so you will know about it right
away.
:::

**9. Read the `count` column before you read the `mean` column. Remember what `.count()` counts:
the non-null `points_final` values, which is finals a country was scored in, not contests it
entered. Three of the seven winners were scored in fewer than four finals. Name them, and say in
one sentence why you would not put any of them in a headline.**

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**France, which tops the 1950s at 19.7 points from 3 scored finals; Serbia, which tops the 2000s
at 214.0 from 2; and Bulgaria, which tops the 2010s at 362.7 from 3.** A mean of two or three
numbers moves by tens of points if a single result is different, so none of the three winners is
stable enough to call a country the best of its decade.

Read the gap between finals and entries while you are here, because it is larger than it looks.
France entered five times in the 1950s and was scored in three, Serbia entered three times in the
2000s and was scored in two, and Bulgaria entered seven times in the 2010s and was scored in
three. Bulgaria's 362.7 is an average of its three best years, and the four years it failed to
qualify contribute nothing to it.

The other four winners are the ones with enough behind them to report: the United Kingdom in the
1960s and 1970s, on 10 finals each, and Ireland in the 1980s and 1990s, on 9 and 10. Three of
the seven decade winners resting on three finals or fewer tells you something about the method
rather than about the countries, because taking the highest mean within a group is exactly the
operation that selects for small counts.
:::

**10. The `mean` column rises from about 20 in the 1950s to about 360 in the 2010s. In a markdown
cell, two or three sentences: is Europe getting better at writing songs? What else changed
between 1956 and 2019 that would produce this pattern? What would you have to divide by to
remove it?**

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**No. The change is in the scale on which points are awarded.** Points come from the competing
countries, and the field grew from about ten entrants in the 1950s to 42 in 2007, so the total
number of points available grew with it. The contest also split the jury vote and the televote
into two separate awards in 2016, which raised the ceiling again: the winning score was 152 in
1975 and 148 in 1995, then 365 in 2015, the last year before the split, and 534 in 2016, the
first year after it. It has stayed in that range since, at 498 in 2019.

To remove the effect you would divide each score by the total points available in that year, or
by the year's winning score, turning an absolute total into a share. A mean of shares can be
compared across decades, while a mean of raw points mostly measures how many countries were
competing.
:::

## Part 4: The second table

**11. Read the population file at
`https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/eurovision_country_populations.csv`.
How many rows, and what are its columns?**

```{python}
pop_url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/eurovision_country_populations.csv'
populations = pd.read_csv(pop_url)

print(populations.shape)
print(list(populations.columns))
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**52 rows and two columns, `country_name` and `population`.** The 52 rows are the 52 countries that
have ever entered, so the population file holds one row per country over the whole history of the
contest, while `contests` holds one row per country per year. The two tables are at different
grains, which is why they need a merge rather than a concatenation.
:::

**12. Build a table called `modern` holding only contests from 1990 onwards, then count the
entries per country and turn that count into a two-column table using the Series-to-table move.
Rename the columns to `country` and `entries`.**

```{python}
modern = contests[contests['year'] >= 1990].copy()

counts = modern['to_country'].value_counts().reset_index()
counts = counts.rename(columns={'to_country': 'country', 'count': 'entries'})

counts.head()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**51 countries, and four of them are at the ceiling of 30: France, the United Kingdom, Spain and
Sweden.** The window 1990 to 2019 holds exactly 30 contests, and no country can enter a contest
twice, so 30 means "entered every single year" and no number in this column can ever exceed it.
Before you read a column of counts, work out the largest value it is allowed to take, because a 30
here means "every year since 1990" rather than just a big number, and a 31 would mean something
had gone wrong in the count.
:::

**13. Merge `counts` with `populations`. The key columns have different names, so you will need
`left_on=` and `right_on=`. Do it twice, once with the default `how=` and once with
`how='right'`, and report both shapes.**

```{python}
entries = pd.merge(counts, populations, left_on='country', right_on='country_name')
check = pd.merge(counts, populations, left_on='country', right_on='country_name', how='right')

print(entries.shape)
print(check.shape)
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**51 rows from the default inner merge and 52 from the right merge, a difference of exactly one
row.** The default `how='inner'` keeps only keys present in both tables, so it returns the 51
countries that have both a modern entry count and a population. `how='right'` keeps every row of
the population file whether or not the left table matched, so the 52nd country arrives with nulls
in its `country` and `entries` columns.

Running the merge a second time, with the right join, is the diagnostic here, because the inner
merge on its own would have told you 51 and given you no way to know that anything had been
dropped.
:::

**14. One country is in the population file and not in your counts. Find it, name it, and then
find every row for it in the full `eurovision` table. In a markdown cell, say what you learned
and why the inner merge was right to drop it.**

```{python}
print(check[check['entries'].isnull()][['country_name', 'population']])
print(eurovision[eurovision['to_country'] == 'Morocco'][['year', 'performer', 'song', 'place_contest']])
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Morocco, population 24,807,462, with exactly one row in the whole file: Samira Bensaïd singing
"Bitakat Hob" in 1980, finishing 18th with 7 points.** Morocco has never returned.

The inner merge was right because `counts` is a table of entries since 1990, and Morocco has none.
Morocco is absent from the `value_counts()` output because `value_counts()` can only count values
that appear, and a country with no rows in `modern` has no value to count. Dropping it keeps the
table honest about what it contains: countries that compete in the modern contest.

The null in the right merge is the subtle part, because it can be read three ways. It does not
mean Morocco's entry count is unknown, and it does not mean the count is zero in general, because
the 1980 entry is real. It means "this key had no match on the left", and you have to decide which
of the three readings applies before you fill anything in. If you had filled it with zero and kept
the row, the entries-per-million table in the next question would include a country that stopped
competing ten years before the window opens.
:::

**15. Add an `entries_per_million` column to `entries`: the entry count divided by the population
in millions. (`1_000_000` is a perfectly good way to write a million in Python; the underscores
are ignored.) Rank it and show the top eight and the bottom five.**

```{python}
entries['entries_per_million'] = entries['entries'] / (entries['population'] / 1_000_000)

ranked = entries.sort_values('entries_per_million', ascending=False)

print(ranked[['country', 'entries', 'population', 'entries_per_million']].head(8))
print(ranked[['country', 'entries', 'population', 'entries_per_million']].tail(5))
```

**16. The top of that ranking is San Marino, Andorra, Iceland, Monaco and Malta, and the bottom
is Yugoslavia, Russia and Serbia & Montenegro. In a markdown cell, three or four sentences: is
*entries per million people* a meaningful quantity? What is it actually measuring, and what
would you have to know about how the file's population numbers were collected before you would
publish this table?**

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**It is arithmetically correct and close to meaningless, because it is almost entirely a ranking
of small populations.** The numerator cannot exceed 30 and falls as low as 2, so it varies by a factor of fifteen
across the table, while the denominator varies by a factor of more than six thousand, from San
Marino at 23,186 to Russia at 148,005,704. Whichever country is smallest will top this ranking
almost regardless of how often it competes: San Marino reaches 431.3 entries per million on only
10 entries, while Russia's 22 entries give 0.149.

The bottom three make the same point from the other end. Yugoslavia sits last at 0.126 on three
entries and Serbia & Montenegro third from last at 0.204 on two, and neither is a country that
competed rarely so much as a country that stopped existing partway through the window. A large population divided into a tiny entry count puts them at the bottom
for a reason that has nothing to do with Eurovision.

The column is really one divided by population, presented as a rate. It says nothing about
enthusiasm per person, because a country sends one entry no matter how many people live in it. The quantity would be meaningful only if the numerator could scale with population,
and here by rule it cannot.

Before publishing it you would need to know what year each population figure is from, and the
file does not say. Iceland is listed at 255,866 and the United Kingdom at 57,247,586, both of
which are roughly late-1980s figures, and the file still has rows for Yugoslavia (23,818,000)
and Serbia & Montenegro (9,791,475), states that ceased to exist in 1992 and 2006. So the
denominators come from mixed and unstated years, and some of them describe countries that did not
exist for most of the 1990 to 2019 window the numerator covers.
:::

## Part 5: The whole contest in one grid

**17. Build a wide table with `to_country` down the rows, `decade` across the columns, and the
mean `points_final` in the cells. What shape is it?**

```{python}
grid = contests.pivot_table(index='to_country', columns='decade', values='points_final')

grid.shape
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**51 rows by 7 columns, one row per country and one column per decade.** The seven columns are the
seven decades, which you already know from question 6.

The 51 is worth a second look, because `contests` holds 52 distinct countries, so one of them is
missing from the grid entirely. Andorra is the missing country: its six entries between 2004 and
2009 never reached a final, so `points_final` is null on every one of them. `pivot_table` drops an
all-null row by default and gives you no warning when it does, so compare the number of rows in a
grid against the number of groups in the data behind it. A grid with fewer rows than that means
some group had nothing to aggregate.
:::

**18. Build the same table again with `aggfunc='count'`, and look at both for four countries that
have competed throughout: Ireland, Sweden, the United Kingdom and Norway.**

```{python}
grid_n = contests.pivot_table(index='to_country', columns='decade',
                              values='points_final', aggfunc='count')

print(grid.loc[['Ireland', 'Sweden', 'United Kingdom', 'Norway']].round(1))
print(grid_n.loc[['Ireland', 'Sweden', 'United Kingdom', 'Norway']])
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**The counts grid counts finals reached, not entries submitted, and the difference shows up after
2004.** Ireland's counts run 5, 10, 9, 10 through the 1990s and then fall to 6 and 5, but Ireland
entered nine times in the 2000s and ten times in the 2010s. The missing entries were eliminated in
the semi-final and so have a null `points_final`. The United Kingdom shows 10 in every full
decade, because the largest financial contributors are seeded straight into the final, a rule that
is not in the file.

The gap between the two grids changes how you read the means. Ireland's 2000s mean of 42.7 is an
average over the six years it qualified, so it leaves out its three worst years by construction,
and it is still the country's weakest decade. Sweden's 2010s mean of 268.3 comes from 9 finals out
of 10 entries. An average computed only over the occasions when a country did well enough to be
scored is biased upward, and the counts grid is where you can see it happening.
:::

**19. In a markdown cell: the empty cells in the means grid are not all the same kind of empty.
Name two different reasons a country might have no number in a given decade, and say how you
would tell them apart using the counts grid.**

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Reason one: the country did not compete in that decade at all.** Ireland in the 1950s and Norway
in the 1950s are examples. Neither country has any rows to aggregate, so both grids are empty in
that cell.

**Reason two: the country competed and never reached a final.** Slovakia in the 2000s and again in
the 2010s, and the Czech Republic, Monaco, Montenegro and San Marino in the 2000s, all entered and
were all eliminated in every semi-final of the decade. Every `points_final` is null, so the mean
is empty, but there were rows to count.

The counts grid separates the two cases: an empty cell there means no entries, while a `0.0` means
entries but no finals. Six cells in the counts grid hold `0.0` where the means grid is empty, and
they are all the second kind of empty. Andorra is a third case, and the one most easily missed,
because it has `0.0` in the counts grid for the 2000s and no row at all in the means grid.

The reading matters because the two look identical in a plot or a report. One says a country was
not there. The other says it was there and never got far enough to be scored, which is a result,
not an absence.
:::

## Part 6: Write it up

There is no single right answer here, but your write-up must cite at least three numbers you
computed, must name at least two distinct reasons the question is harder than it sounds, and must
end with the table or number you would actually send. Here is one answer that would earn full
marks.

:::{.callout-note title="✅ A model answer"}
Partly, and only for a period that ended twenty years ago. Ireland has the highest average
`points_final` of any country in both the 1980s and the 1990s, at 99.2 points from 9 finals and
119.2 from 10, and both of those rows rest on enough entries to mean something, which is more than
three of the seven decade winners can say. On that evidence Ireland was the strongest country of
two consecutive decades, a run only the United Kingdom matches, in the 1960s and 1970s.

The claim stops being supportable as soon as it is extended to "in history", for two reasons. The
first is that points are not comparable across eras. The field grew from 26 entries in 2003 to 36
in 2004 when the semi-final was introduced, and the winning score rose from 148 in 1995 to 498 in
2019, so a raw mean rewards recency rather than quality. The second is that the counts grid shows
Ireland reaching only 6 finals in the 2000s and 5 in the 2010s, and its mean in those decades,
42.7 and 66.2, is an average over its better years alone, because the years it failed to qualify
contribute nothing. Sweden's 268.3 in the 2010s is on the same inflated scale and cannot be set
against Ireland's 119.2 from the 1990s.

The data cannot tell the editor who is best overall, because no common scale exists. I would send
the two pivot tables together, means beside counts, for the countries that competed throughout,
and the sentence that goes with them: Ireland dominated the 1980s and 1990s, and the
question of the best country in history is not answerable from points.
:::

## Where the marks are

When you compare your notebook against this key, check these four things before anything else.

1. **Did you run both merges and compare 51 to 52?** The single dropped row was the whole point of
   question 13, and an inner merge on its own gives you no signal that anything went missing.
2. **Did you read the `count` column before the `mean` column, every time?** Three of the seven
   decade winners rest on fewer than four scored finals, and in Part 5 the counts grid is what
   tells you that Ireland's later means were computed over qualifying years only.
3. **Can you tell the two kinds of empty cell apart?** A null in the means grid with `0.0` beside
   it in the counts grid is a country that competed and never made a final. A null in both is a
   country that was not there.
4. **Did you keep away from `.fillna(0)`?** Using it on 2020 would have given you 41 real scores of
   zero, and using it on the merge would have put a country that last competed in 1980 into a
   table about the modern contest.
